title: Inflation: What Is Measured and What Moves It
summary: How a price index is built, why core and headline diverge, and the one calculation that decides whether a return was real.

lesson.body:
[[inflation|Inflation]] is a sustained rise in the general price level. Not one price going up — the whole level, so that a unit of currency buys less than it did.

Measuring it means choosing a basket. A [[cpi|consumer price index]] tracks the cost of a fixed basket of what households actually buy, weighted by how much they spend on each item. Housing is a third or so of the basket in most developed economies; food, transport, medical care and everything else split the rest.

Three things follow immediately from "a weighted basket":

**The weights decide the answer.** A 5% rise in a 33% weight moves the index more than a 15% rise in a 5% weight.

**Your inflation rate is not the index.** A renter in a city, a car commuter and a retiree have different baskets. The index is an average nobody experiences exactly.

**The basket has to be updated, and updating it changes the series.** Substitution, quality adjustment and new products are all judgement calls with real effects on the printed number.

**Headline inflation includes everything. Core inflation excludes food and energy.**

The exclusion looks like a dodge — those are the prices people notice most. The reason is signal, not comfort: energy and food prices are volatile and driven by weather, harvests and geopolitics rather than by domestic demand. A spike that reverses in six months tells a [[central-bank|central bank]] nothing about the pressure it can actually influence.

So the split has a clean division of labour:

**Headline is what people experience** and what wage demands respond to. It is the honest measure of purchasing power.

**Core is what policy responds to**, because it is a better guide to where inflation goes next.

**The trap is that the exclusion only works if the spike really does reverse.** When energy stays high long enough to feed into transport costs, food production and wage bargaining, it stops being noise and becomes exactly what core was trying to measure. Second-round effects are the reason "look through it" is a judgement rather than a rule.

**Every return figure you will ever be shown is nominal unless it explicitly says otherwise, and inflation is the difference between a return and a result.**

A fund returns 6% in a year when inflation was 4%. The investor is about 2% better off, not 6%. Over a decade, that gap compounds into a completely different outcome: 6% nominal for ten years multiplies capital by 1.79, while the real figure — call it 1.92% — multiplies purchasing power by 1.21.

This is the [[real-interest-rate|real rate]] logic applied to any return, and it is why **the single most useful question about a long-horizon investment is what it does when inflation is high, not what it returns on average.**

It also explains an oddity of the alternatives world. [[real-assets|Real assets]], [[infrastructure]] with inflation-linked revenue and [[floating-rate|floating-rate]] credit are all sold on inflation protection, and they are genuinely different from each other: one owns the thing whose price is rising, one has a contractual escalator, and one has a coupon that resets. The first two protect the asset's real value; the third protects income while inflation is high and gives it back when rates fall.

lesson.plainReading: One plus the real return equals one plus the nominal return, divided by one plus inflation. Subtracting inflation from the nominal rate is the shortcut, and it is close enough only while both numbers are small.

variables.meaning: the return or interest rate as quoted
the inflation rate over the same period

lesson.body: A simplified basket: housing 33%, transport 17%, food 14%, everything else 36%. Over the year housing rose 5%, transport fell 3%, food rose 2%, everything else rose 3%. A [[policy-rate|policy rate]] of 5.25% sits against the result.
walkthrough: Weighted contribution, item by item: housing 0.33 × 5% = **1.65pp**; transport 0.17 × −3% = **−0.51pp**; food 0.14 × 2% = **0.28pp**; other 0.36 × 3% = **1.08pp**.
Now notice what did the work. Housing alone contributed 1.65pp of the 2.50pp — **two thirds of the total from one third of the basket.**
And transport falling 3% held the index down by half a point. Remove that one favourable line and headline is 3.01% instead of 2.50%.

**Read that carefully: the headline number is one line item away from a different policy conversation.** This is why the composition of an inflation print matters more than its level, and why the market reaction to a print often ignores the headline entirely.
Against the 5.25% policy rate, the real policy rate is 1.0525 / 1.0250 − 1 = **2.68%**. The quick subtraction gives 2.75%, close enough here and not at higher inflation.

Sanity check worth reusing: **contributions must sum to the headline.** If someone shows you an inflation decomposition whose parts do not add up to the printed number, something has been dropped — usually the line that undermines the argument.

lesson.caption: Where inflation comes from, and what each kind implies
rows: Spending exceeds what the economy can supply — a positive [[output-gap|output gap]]
Policy works: raising rates reduces demand. This is the case rate rises are designed for.
An input price shock — energy, shipping, a harvest failure
Policy is nearly powerless on the cause. Raising rates cannot produce more oil; it can only stop the shock spreading.
Wages chase prices which chase wages
The outcome policy fears most, because it becomes self-sustaining and expensive to stop.
People plan for higher inflation and act accordingly
The reason central banks talk so much. Anchored expectations are an asset that took decades to build.

lesson.body:
**Reading a [[base-effect|base effect]] as news.** An annual rate compares this month with the same month a year ago. If that month was unusually low, the annual rate jumps with nothing happening now. Base effects are arithmetic, not information, and they are entirely predictable in advance.

**Annualising a monthly print.** A 0.4% month is roughly 4.9% annualised — a real signal, but one month of a noisy series. The convention flatters big numbers in both directions.

**Confusing a price level with a rate.** Inflation falling from 9% to 3% does not mean prices fell. The level is still far above where it started, which is why "inflation is beaten" and "everything is expensive" are both true at once and constantly talked past each other.

**Assuming an inflation hedge works at all horizons.** Equities are a decent long-run inflation hedge and a poor short-run one; they fall when inflation surprises upward, then grow into it. Commodities work when commodities *are* the inflation and not otherwise. [[deflation|Deflation]] breaks other assumptions entirely — debt gets heavier in real terms rather than lighter.

**Ignoring the hedged currency of your inflation.** A European investor's purchasing power depends on European prices. A US-focused inflation hedge protects against the wrong index.

**"Inflation-protected" is a marketing phrase covering at least four different mechanisms, and the differences decide whether it works.**

*Contractual linkage* — revenue explicitly indexed to a published index. The strongest form, and it comes with caps, lags and floors that must be read.

*Pricing power* — the firm can raise prices because customers have nowhere else to go. Real but conditional on competition and on demand holding up.

*Owning the thing* — commodities and real assets, where the asset's price is part of the index. Works when the inflation is commodity-driven.

*Rate reset* — floating-rate credit, where coupons rise as policy rates rise. Protects income, not principal, and only while rates stay high.

One question separates them: **when inflation rose 6% last year, what happened to this asset's revenue, and was it a contract or a hope?**

**Ask which index a contractual escalator uses, with what lag and what cap.** "CPI-linked" with a 2% cap in a 7% inflation year is 2% linked and 5% unprotected. The cap is the number that matters and it is usually in the schedule rather than the summary.

**Ask what the actual revenue increase was last year, in percent.** Not the mechanism — the outcome. A manager who cannot produce it for a portfolio sold on inflation linkage has not tested the claim either.

**Ask whether returns quoted for a long-dated strategy are real or nominal.** For anything over ten years the difference dominates. If the answer is nominal, ask what inflation assumption sits inside the model.

**For floating-rate credit, ask what happens to borrower coverage as rates rise.** The coupon rises for you and the interest bill rises for them. Protection that pushes your borrowers toward default is not protection.

**Check whether the hedge matches your own currency's inflation.** For a non-US investor, a US-linked instrument protects the wrong basket.

items: A price index is a weighted basket, so composition beats level: in the worked example one third of the basket produced two thirds of the inflation.
Core excludes food and energy for signal, not comfort — and the exclusion only holds while the spike genuinely reverses rather than feeding into wages.
Real return = (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) − 1. Subtracting is a shortcut that fails as inflation rises, and 6% nominal at 4% inflation is a 1.9% result.
"Inflation-protected" covers contractual linkage, pricing power, owning the asset and rate resets. Ask which one, and what the revenue actually did last year.

questions.stem: Basket weights: housing 33%, transport 17%, food 14%, other 36%. Housing +5%, transport −3%, food +2%, other +3%. What is headline inflation, in percent?
questions.inputHint: Sum each weight times its price change.
questions.explanation: Worth noticing which line did the work: housing contributed 1.65 of the 2.50. When a print surprises, the first move is always to look at the contributions rather than the total — the total is an average of things that have nothing to do with each other.

questions.stem: A fund returned 6.0% in a year when inflation was 4.0%. What was the real return, in percent, using the exact relationship?
questions.explanation: The subtraction shortcut gives 2.00% — close, and the gap widens fast with inflation. At 20% nominal and 15% inflation the shortcut says 5% and the exact answer is 4.35%, which is a 13% overstatement of the real result.

questions.stem: Why do central banks watch core inflation rather than headline?
choices: Because food and energy prices are not part of the cost of living
Because food and energy are volatile and driven by supply shocks, so they are a poor guide to where inflation goes next
Because core inflation is always lower
Because headline inflation is not published frequently enough
rationales: They plainly are — headline is the honest measure of what households experience. The exclusion is about forecasting, not about relevance.
Correct. The excluded items are noisy and largely outside domestic policy's influence, so core is the better signal for what policy can actually affect.
Core has run above headline in plenty of periods, particularly when energy prices were falling.
Both are published monthly in most economies.
questions.explanation: The corollary matters more than the rule: because the justification is "it will reverse", core stops being the right measure the moment an energy shock persists long enough to reach wages. That is a judgement call every cycle, and it is where central banks make their most consequential mistakes.

questions.stem: Annual inflation jumps from 2.1% to 3.4% in one month, but the monthly price change was in line with the previous six months. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: A sudden demand surge in that month
A base effect — the month dropping out of the twelve-month window was unusually weak
A change in the basket weights
A data error that will be revised away
rationales: The monthly change was normal, so nothing surged now. The move came from the comparison, not from current prices.
Correct. An annual rate compares now with a year ago. When a weak month drops out of the window, the annual figure rises with nothing happening today — and it is entirely predictable in advance.
Reweighting happens on a schedule and produces small, announced effects, not a 1.3pp jump.
Possible in principle, but a normal monthly print plus a jumping annual rate is the signature of a base effect, not an error.
questions.explanation: The practical upshot: month-on-month annualised tells you what is happening now and annual tells you what has happened over a year. Anyone reacting to an annual rate without checking the base month is reacting to arithmetic from twelve months ago.

questions.stem: "Inflation has fallen from 9% to 3%, so prices are coming back down." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — a lower inflation rate means prices are rising more slowly, not falling; the level stays where the earlier inflation left it
False — prices only fall when inflation goes below zero, which would be good news
True — a falling inflation rate means falling prices
False — because the 9% figure would have been revised by now
rationales: Correct. Rate versus level, again. After a year at 9% and a year at 3%, prices are about 12% above where they started and still climbing, just gently.
The right distinction but the wrong verdict on deflation — falling prices are generally bad news, because debt becomes heavier in real terms and spending gets postponed.
This is the misconception under test, and it is behind most of the gap between official statistics and public perception.
Revisions to inflation are small and would not change the conclusion.
questions.explanation: This is the same flow-versus-stock confusion that makes GDP paradoxical, in a different costume. Inflation is a rate of change; the price level is the accumulated stock. Central banks target the rate, and households experience the level — which is why both sides of that argument are right.

questions.stem: An infrastructure fund is marketed as inflation-protected through CPI-linked contracts. Inflation was 7%. What is the most revealing question?
choices: What is the fund's target return?
What did portfolio revenue actually rise by last year, and what caps and lags apply to the linkage?
How long are the remaining contract terms?
rationales: The target is a statement of intent and is unaffected by whether the linkage worked.
Correct. The outcome tests the mechanism. A 2% cap in a 7% year delivers 2% of linkage and 5% of erosion, and caps live in the schedules rather than the summary.
Relevant detail, and a distant second: which index matters far less than whether the escalator was capped.
Important for durability, but it does not tell you whether the protection functioned when tested.
questions.explanation: The pattern recurs across every claimed hedge: ask for the realised outcome in the year the hedge was needed, not the description of how it is supposed to work. One year of realised revenue growth settles arguments that a term sheet cannot.

questions.stem: A direct lending fund argues floating-rate loans make it inflation-protected. What is the strongest objection?
choices: Floating rates do not actually rise with inflation
Rising coupons raise borrowers' interest costs at the same time, so the protection increases credit risk in the portfolio it is protecting
Floating-rate loans have no principal protection
Interest rate rises lag inflation by too long to matter
rationales: They rise with the reference rate, which does typically rise with inflation. The mechanism works; the objection is elsewhere.
Correct. The same rate rise that lifts your income lifts the borrower's bill. Protection that pushes leveraged borrowers toward breaching coverage covenants is protection with a self-inflicted cost.
True of most credit and not specific to floating rates — a fixed-rate loan has the same principal risk plus duration risk.
Reference rates move with policy rates, which respond to inflation with a lag measured in months, not years.
questions.explanation: Worth generalising: whenever an asset is described as hedged, ask who is on the other side of the hedge and whether you also own their risk. In direct lending you own both the coupon and the borrower, which makes the two effects impossible to separate.
